'''''Aegilops triuncialis''''', or '''barbed goatgrass''', is a grass species of the family [[Poaceae]].<ref name=Cal-IPC /> It is a [[winter annual]] native to many areas in [[Eastern Europe|Eastern]] and [[Mediterranean Europe]] and [[Western Asia]].<ref name="Davy J" />  It is considered an [[introduced species|introduced]], [[invasive species]] in North America, mainly in the Western coast of the United States.<ref name=ODA>{{cite web|last=Oregon Department of Agriculture|title=barbed goatgrass (aegilops triuncialis L.)|url=http://www.oregon.gov/ODA/PLANT/weeds/Pages/profile_barbedgoatgrass.aspx|access-date=6 March 2014}}</ref> In its native lands, the grass thrives in mainly rocky, [[serpentine soil]], but also does well in [[grasslands]] and [[ruderal]]/[[disturbed ground]] as well as [[oak woodland]]s.<ref name=issg /><ref name="Rice K">{{cite journal|last=Rice|first=Kevin|title=Evolutionary ecology along invasion fronts of the annual grass Aegilops triuncialis|journal=Biological Invasions|date=November 1, 2013|volume=15|issue=11|pages=2531–2545|doi=10.1007/s10530-013-0471-6|bibcode=2013BiInv..15.2531R |s2cid=10393646|url=https://escholarship.org/content/qt8q67s2br/qt8q67s2br.pdf?t=mwvmll}}</ref>

==Description==
Barbed goatgrass grows to be about {{convert|8|to|16|in|cm|0}} tall with few to many rigid, loosely erect aerial stems (culms).<ref name=ODA />  In late spring the plant produces rigid flower spikes consisting of three to six spikelets bearing long, stiff [[Awn (botany)|awns]] which assist in seed distribution. When the grass matures, the spikelets fall off in their entirety to [[germinate]] on the ground,<ref name="Davy J" /> and the long awns which give the plant its name assist in dispersal by animals, wind or water.<ref name=issg>{{cite web|title=Aegilops triuncialis (grass)|url=http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=1691|website=Global Invasive Species Database|access-date=11 October 2015|archive-date=31 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160131091225/http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=1691|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==As an invasive species==
Barbed goatgrass was introduced to North America in the 20th century from Mediterranean Europe and Western Asia.<ref name="Davy J" />  It has been found in California, Oregon, Nevada, and the New England area, but with the greatest impact in California.<ref name=issg /><ref name="ODA, Risk" />  Barbed goatgrass was introduced to the California area with the trade of Mexican cattle in the early 20th century.<ref name="ODA, Risk">{{cite journal|last=French|first=Ken|title=Plant Pest Risk Assessment for Barbed and Ovate Goatgrass, Aegilops triuncialis, A. geniculata|journal=Plant Pest Risk Assessment, ODA|year=2010|pages=1–11|url=http://www.oregon.gov/ODA/PLANT/WEEDS/docs/pdf/ra_barbedgoatgrass2013.pdf|access-date=6 March 2014}}</ref> The plant's unusual ability to invade nutrient-depleted, infertile soils means that it can severely damage habitats which often serve as important [[Refugium (population biology)|refugia]] for endemic grassland species which most other invading grasses are unable to exploit.<ref name=issg/>

Barbed goatgrass is a fast-growing, rapidly spreading invasive species mainly in grasslands, pastures, and ranches. It is listed as a [[noxious weed]] by [[California Department of Food and Agriculture]].<ref name=Merenlender>{{cite web|last=Merenlender|first=Adina|title=Successful Burning Strategy to Control Barbed Goatgrass|url=http://ucanr.edu/sites/oak_range/Oak_Articles_On_Line/Oaks_and_Fire/Successful_Burning_Strategy_to_Control_Barbed_Goatgrass_692/|publisher=University of California, Oak Woodland Management|access-date=1 April 2014}}</ref> Because of its fast, invasive growing patterns, barbed goatgrass creates a [[monoculture]], killing the other plants in its area.<ref name="Davy J" />  The invasive nature of barbed goatgrass is causing a decrease in [[species diversity]], and a decrease in [[forage]].<ref name="Davy J">{{cite journal|last=Davy|first=Josh|title=Barbed Goatgrass|journal=ANR Publication|date=October 2008|volume=8315|pages=1–5|url=http://anrcatalog.ucdavis.edu/pdf/8315.pdf|access-date=6 March 2014|archive-date=11 June 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140611155841/http://anrcatalog.ucdavis.edu/pdf/8315.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> Most grazing animals tend to avoid barbed goatgrass because they do not like the taste of it, allowing the grass to take over the other grasses and grains consumed by the animals.<ref name="ODA, Risk" />  The barbs on the flower spikelets containing the seeds become attached easily to animal fur, human clothing, and vehicles which allows the seeds to become more widely dispersed over the area.<ref name="Davy J" />

==Control methods==
The most important component in the control of barbed goatgrass is early detection. When found in small isolated areas, it can be taken care of more effectively.<ref name="Davy J" /> A recently developed method of assessing greenness in aerial color infrared (CIR) imagery using Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) values to differentiate between these invasive weedy grasses and other more innocuous species may help land managers with early detection.<ref name="Malmstrom, C.M. 2017">Malmstrom, C.M., H.S. Butterfield, L. Planck, C.W. Long, and V.T. Eviner. (2017). Novel fine-scale aerial mapping approach quantifies grassland weed cover dynamics and response to management. PLOS ONE  12(10): e0181665.</ref> Barbed goatgrass matures in late spring after most other annual grasses have already senesced, and this method utilizes these differences in phenology to easily identify patches that require management.

[[Controlled burning]] is one method being used by the [[University of California]] in small areas to try to control the amount of barbed goatgrass.<ref name="Davy J" /> To be most effective, multiple burns had to be performed in the isolated area over two years to more fully rid the area of the grass. After the burns, many [[native species]] were able to live in the small area once again.<ref name="Davy J" /><ref name=Merenlender />

Another control method used by the University of California to control barbed goatgrass is the spraying of [[glyphosate]]. Used over a two-year period in small areas, glyphosate was able kill barbed goatgrass and all its seedlings.<ref name="Davy J" /><ref name=Aigner /> Although the chemical is effective in killing barbed goatgrass, it also kills the other plants in the area.<ref name="Davy J" /><ref name=Aigner>{{cite journal|last=Aigner|first=Paul|title=Herbicides and Mowing to Control Barb Goatgrass|journal=Invasive Plant Science and Management|volume=4|issue=4|pages=448–457|doi=10.1614/IPSM-D-11-00027.1|year=2011|s2cid=84215887}}</ref> [[Aminocyclopyrachlor]], a new experimental chemical is being used to control barbed goatgrass by the University of California's Weed Science department. It has been shown to be extremely effective, however, aminocyclopyrachlor is not a registered [[herbicide]] and as such, widespread use is not yet allowed.<ref name=Kyser>{{cite web|last=Kyser|first=Guy|title=Selective control of barb goatgrass with aminocyclopyrachlor|url=http://ucanr.edu/blogs/blogcore/postdetail.cfm?postnum=7868|publisher=UC Weed Science|access-date=1 April 2014}}</ref>

[[Mowing]] of the grass is another control method. It allows the grass to be cut before maturing and developing seeds to reproduce, but it is not as effective as the other methods as the deep and established root system of the barbed goatgrass is still in place and can grow again.<ref name="Davy J" /><ref name=Aigner />

==Impact on humans==
Although there are many ways to control the growth of barbed goatgrass, a real solution has not been found in its widespread prevention. Barbed goatgrass [[cross breed]]s with different types of [[wheat]], causing the grain to become [[Sterility (physiology)|infertile]] and unusable for harvest, which hurts the economy of the rural California areas.<ref name=ODA /> It can also seriously harm grazing animals by the barbs becoming embedded in their nose, mouth, and eyes, causing farmers and ranchers extra expenses.<ref name="Davy J" />  It reduces the amount of forage in the area, decreases biodiversity and overall degrades the ecosystem it resides in.<ref name="Davy J" /> Studies of the University of California also show that if climate change increased the amount of precipitation in the area, the amount of barbed goatgrass may increase, destroying even more of its ecosystem.<ref name=Morrison>{{cite web|last=Morrison|first=Elise|title=The effects of climate change on the growth of barbed goatgrass|url=http://www.cal-ipc.org/symposia/archive/pdf/2010/3Morrison.pdf|publisher=University of California|access-date=1 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140407084923/http://www.cal-ipc.org/symposia/archive/pdf/2010/3Morrison.pdf|archive-date=7 April 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> Its rapid growth and resiliency against control methods prove that barbed goatgrass is an invasive species that could cause many more problems to the agriculture of California and possibly many other areas if it is not taken care of soon.<ref name="Davy J" />
